models.best: Inferred from its principle that contributions to the common stock are given as gifts that create a duty to return, so the burden is shared through obligation and trust rather than through fixed rates. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a gift creates an obligation to return, so contributions follow status and alliances rather than any fixed measure, and outsiders without allies carry a larger share of the common burden. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Sahlins, Stone Age Economics (1972)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances its work against its needs, so a levy is sized to household labour and consumption and takes only what the family can spare. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so a fixed charge larger than a household's spare output forces its members to work longer or sell stock to pay it, and small households with few workers bear it hardest. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy (1925)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the centre collects tribute and taxes in goods, stores them and pays workers and officials from one common store, so the burden is pooled across the whole community. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case EU VAT gap, the shortfall against expected VAT, measures what a collector expects but does not receive. A newspaper report of the European Commission's figures put the 2022 gap at €89.3bn, about 7% of expected VAT, and that total absorbs avoidance, bankruptcy losses and calculation mistakes, so it is wider than evasion alone. A later trade report gives €101bn for 2022, so the sources disagree. Inferred from its principle that a shortfall leaves the common store smaller than planned. Source: Law Society Gazette (Ireland), December 2024, reporting the European Commission's VAT gap report (2022 data); later trade coverage (Shared Services Link, February 2026)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, so the state's revenue rests on trade and on the property of owners, with no levy on wages because the labour is owned rather than paid. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through ownership, so the enslaved, denied property, hold no assets that a tax could reach, and the costs of the state fall on the output of their labour. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe fixed labour services and rents in return for land, protection and justice, so obligations are known in advance and the manor supplies most of its own needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are owed to a lord, so dues fall due whatever the harvest, and a tenant who falls short has no means to change the terms, since the lord also supplies the justice on the manor. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939-1940)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes fix fees for entry and training, so the trade pays for its own training through published charges rather than through levies set by an outside authority. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry and statutes fix charges, so admission fees fall hardest on journeymen and apprentices with the least capital, and those who cannot pay are kept out of the trade. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth (2000)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims for a trade surplus, so duties on imports and on colonial trade raise revenue and build reserves of gold, while production at home is favoured. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trade is regulated for a surplus, so duties on imports and charges on colonial goods raise prices for buyers at home, and the cost of the surplus falls on consumers under rules that the state sets. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism (1935)

models.best: The case Denmark's municipal land tax (grundskyld) levies land and leaves buildings out of its base, funding services such as schools and roads, which is the closest case to a single tax on the rent of land. It is one tax among several, unlike the single land tax of Physiocracy, and its material is mostly older, so current rates are unconfirmed.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land is the only tax, so the state's revenue rests on land rents alone, and any fall in those rents leaves the state short while the tax reaches only landowners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy (1962)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state protects property and contracts and otherwise stays out, so taxes are few and fund only that protection, and wages and profits are left to competition. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state stays out, so the few taxes that remain must pay for the protection of property and contracts, and a small budget leaves no room to ease the charges that fall on those with the least income. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so taxes that leave prices and profits free to signal, and that do not fund planning or credit expansion, let production follow what buyers need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that state planning and credit expansion distort production, so taxes that fund planning, and credit expansion of any kind, push output into projects that prices would not support, and taxpayers carry the cost of that misdirected output. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)

models.best: The case Repeal of net wealth taxes in Europe and the OECD lists early repeals, including Austria's in 1994 and Sweden's in 2007, which fits a smaller state with lower levies on capital. These are secondary summaries only, and they disagree on how to classify France's 2018 change.
models.worst: The case US top federal income tax rate, 1913 to 1987 reports a fall from 77% to below 40% between 1964 and 1987. Inferred from its principle that a smaller state takes less from top incomes, cuts of that kind lower how progressive the tax is. An Economic Policy Institute chart ties a rise in the top 1% pre-tax income share to steep top-rate cuts, but that link is the chart's own framing, not a result, and both sources are secondary. Source: Wolters Kluwer, historical income tax rates explainer (updated 29 April 2026); Economic Policy Institute, chart of top marginal rate and top 1% income share (year not stated)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that taxes move against government spending, so they rise in booms and ease in slumps, keeping demand and employment high. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that taxes move the other way from spending, so a tax rise in a slump, or a tax cut in a boom, pulls demand against the cycle and leaves fewer people in work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory (1936)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that social insurance sits within a legal order that curbs monopoly, so levies on pay and firms fund protection against illness and job loss, and the same rules apply to every competitor. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that social insurance and worker representation are tied to firms and jobs, so people outside steady employment pay in less or go without cover, and levies tied to pay reach only those in work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft (1947)

models.best: The model's principle is financing universal public services by high taxes, and the case Tax take in Denmark, Sweden and the United States puts 2024 tax take at about 45.2% of GDP in Denmark, about 41.4% in Sweden and about 25.6% in the United States. These come from secondary summaries, the source page was not read in full, and definitions can differ, while the figures measure taxes raised, not spending.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that financing by high taxes depends on collecting what is due. The case EU VAT gap, the shortfall against expected VAT, measures revenue that is expected but not received: a newspaper report of the European Commission's figures put the 2022 gap at €89.3bn, about 7% of expected VAT, across the EU as a whole. That total absorbs avoidance, bankruptcy losses and calculation mistakes, so it is wider than evasion alone. A later trade report gives €101bn for 2022, so the sources disagree. Source: Law Society Gazette (Ireland), December 2024, reporting the European Commission's VAT gap report (2022 data); later trade coverage (Shared Services Link, February 2026)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries, so tax relief and levies follow export results and reward firms that meet their targets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit and tax relief are directed to chosen industries, so firms outside those sectors carry more of the tax burden, and favoured firms are shielded from the levies that others pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982)

models.best: The case Denmark's municipal land tax (grundskyld) levies land and leaves buildings out of its base, funding services such as schools and roads, which matches the model's aim of taxing land rather than what is built on it. It is one tax among several, and its material is mostly older, so current rates are unconfirmed.
models.worst: The case Pittsburgh's split-rate land tax taxed land above buildings from 1913. The split rate was dropped in 2001, after a county reassessment showed that land values had been under-assessed and tax bills rose. Inferred from its principle that a tax on land value raises less when values lag the market. The findings come from secondary summaries that disagree on the 1913 start and on the 1979 and 1980 ratios, and several sources read as advocacy-leaning. Source: Oates and Schwab, The Impact of Urban Land Taxation: The Pittsburgh Experience, National Tax Journal (1997), as reported in secondary summaries; Mark Hughes, University of Pennsylvania (2005)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities, built by example, fund their shared needs from their own product, so no separate tax on wages is needed and surpluses are shared among members. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities replace wage competition by voluntary example, so shared costs rest on members who choose to contribute, and when contributions fall short the burden lands on those who keep paying. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel (1829)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers keep the full value of their work, with banks lending at cost and rent on property abolished, so there is no property rent to tax and levies that would take from wages fall away. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts and mutual credit replace a central levy, so shared services such as roads or courts depend on agreement among members, and a group that declines to pay leaves the service unfunded. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property? (1840)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control the firm and share its surplus between users and workers, so taxes on the enterprise fall on a surplus its members share, and no outside owner draws a return. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that one member one vote governs the firm, so a majority of members can set the levy on the enterprise, and members who are outvoted, or who are not members, carry burdens set by others. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives (from 1956)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no wages, so no tax is levied, and federated communes share goods by need with no charge for what each person takes. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, so nothing is levied to pay for shared defence, courts or care for those who cannot work, and the cost of those services falls on members' voluntary labour. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread (1892)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations run industry directly, so the costs of running it are met from member dues and the enterprises' own earnings rather than from a levy set outside the workplace. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes, and eventually a general strike, are the means of change, so public revenue falls when a strike spreads, and the cost of the stoppage lands on the public and on workers who are not members. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail (1902)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public enterprise and a national minimum of welfare are paid for through democratic votes and in gradual steps, so the surplus of public enterprise and taxes approved by voters fund the minimum. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that enterprise and welfare are public, so the losses of public enterprise, and the cost of the national minimum, fall on taxpayers, and a gradual approach may leave revenue short for years before the minimum is met. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the Fabian Society (1884)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, so levies on an industry are set by its councils, and the state takes a share as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state is one partner among several, so the revenue from an industry depends on the councils' agreement, and a council that refuses a levy leaves the state's share unfunded while the others carry on. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry (1917)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output, prices and investment, so the state collects its revenue at the point of sale on goods whose prices it sets, and funds investment directly from the budget. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case Turnover tax in the Soviet budget during the war reports the turnover tax's share of budget revenue falling from 73.3% to 49.6% by late 1941, as wartime conditions curbed consumer purchases. The source is a short secondary write-up of archival research, and its baseline year is not given, so the 73.3% share cannot be placed in time. Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and prices, a budget that leans on a levy on consumer purchases weakens when those purchases are curbed. Source: Higher School of Economics (HSE), write-up of Oleg Khlevnyuk's archival research (year not stated)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public firms follow market prices and a central board sets investment, so the state's revenue comes from charges on enterprise profit and capital, which keeps market prices as the guide. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules, so a charge on enterprises can be set unevenly between firms, and managers who follow market prices can face charges that the board changes after they have acted on the old rules. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Yugoslav workers' self-management (1950s)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that once the state withers away and classes disappear, distribution follows ability and need, so taxes give way to shared funds that pay people by need, and no class draws income from another. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state must first wither away, so taxes and levies continue through the transition, and the principle does not say how that burden is set, which leaves the rates to the same state that is expected to disappear. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that key sectors stay in public ownership alongside markets, so the state keeps the revenue of those sectors and shares the rest between centre and regions under rules set by the leadership, phased in gradually. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: China's 1994 tax-sharing reform kept 75% of VAT for the centre and gave local governments the other 25% of VAT and the business tax. One paper concludes it did not reach its potential target. The central share of total fiscal revenue was below 50% from 1996 to 1998, and expanding local extra-budgetary funds pushed down the central share of disposable revenue, so total-revenue shares should not be read alone. These are secondary descriptions not tied to named documents, and legal rates need checking in the original documents. Source: IMF working paper (2004) and academic articles on the 1994 reform, including a 1997 academic article that gives the same VAT split

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils agree shared contributions through repeated proposals, so the cost of public goods is set by those who use and do the work, not by a planner or by market prices. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan through repeated proposals, so decisions on shared levies may take many rounds, and public goods can go unfunded while proposals are argued. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward (1991)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, so levies on industry are collected through the corporations in one channel, and the state sets those rates to serve the national goals it chooses. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry towards national goals, including war, so tax revenue and levies are steered towards those goals, and workers and firms with no independent voice in the corporations carry the burden. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law (1934)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that zakat redistributes wealth, so a levy on wealth paid by owners reaches those in need, and finance that shares profit and risk spreads the loss between lenders and borrowers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trust underpins contracts, so zakat depends on the trust of those who pay it and of the bodies that distribute it, and where that trust is weak, levies collected may not reach those in need. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System (1985)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that moderate consumption and small-scale local production are the aim, so taxes fall lightly on small local producers and more heavily on large-scale, high-volume consumption. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, so a flat levy designed with large producers in mind would bear hardest on small local producers, and a tax on consumption could weigh most on those with the fewest choices. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful (1973)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread property and small enterprise are the aim, so taxes fall lightly on small holdings and are raised and spent by the smallest body competent to do so, keeping decisions close to the people they affect. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that wide property is the aim, so a tax code written for large firms, or a central levy on property, would bear hardest on small holdings and could push them towards larger owners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State (1912)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic activity stays within planetary limits, so taxes fall on resource use and pollution rather than on labour, and the proceeds fund a social floor under everyone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so the tax base may shrink as activity falls, and a social floor funded from a shrinking base may leave gaps in the cover it promises. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Raworth, Doughnut Economics (2017)

models.best: The case Denmark's municipal land tax (grundskyld) is a levy on land that leaves buildings out of its base, and secondary summaries report that land tax is by far the largest share of local property-tax revenue, though its material is mostly older and it is one tax among several. Inferred from its principle that land taxes pay for the income, a land base can carry much of the revenue.
models.worst: The case Pittsburgh's split-rate land tax taxed land above buildings from 1913, and its split rate was dropped in 2001, after a county reassessment showed land values had been under-assessed. Inferred from its principle that a universal payment is funded from land taxes, a base that lags the market raises less until it is corrected. The findings come from secondary summaries that disagree on the 1913 start and on the 1979 and 1980 ratios, and several sources read as advocacy-leaning. Source: Oates and Schwab, The Impact of Urban Land Taxation: The Pittsburgh Experience, National Tax Journal (1997), as reported in secondary summaries; Mark Hughes, University of Pennsylvania (2005)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment, so taxes serve to restrain inflation and shape demand and distribution rather than to pay for spending. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, so spending that outruns what the economy can supply pushes prices up, and taxes that do not respond to that rise leave the adjustment to prices. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that users design, monitor and enforce their own rules, so the fees and levies that pay for upkeep are set by the users, who see the cost of the resource directly. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities enforce their own rules inside wider institutions, so levies on use may fall unevenly on members with less say, and where local rules cannot hold, the wider institutions must enforce them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990)

compromise.summary: The design raises revenue from several bases: a levy on land value pays for local services with buildings left out, a tax take broad enough to fund universal services, and rates that rise in booms and ease in slumps. No single consumer levy carries the budget, and each base has a published check.
compromise.details: Keeps: a land levy that leaves buildings out and funds local services (Georgism; Denmark's municipal land tax (grundskyld)); a tax take broad enough for universal services (Nordic social democracy; Tax take in Denmark, Sweden and the United States); rates that rise in booms and ease in slumps (Keynesian welfare capitalism, inferred). Blocks: under-assessed land, by yearly revaluation (Pittsburgh's split-rate land tax); VAT leakage, by yearly reconciliation (EU VAT gap, the shortfall against expected VAT); one consumer levy carrying the budget, by a cap on any one tax's share (Turnover tax in the Soviet budget during the war); steep top-rate cuts, by a progressivity review first (US top federal income tax rate, 1913 to 1987). Test: over a full economic cycle, the share of land revalued, the VAT gap, the largest tax's share of revenue and the top rate's progressivity. Source: OECD seminar presentation (2000); Tax Foundation (2024); Law Society Gazette (2024); Oates and Schwab (1997); Higher School of Economics write-up; Wolters Kluwer explainer (2026); Keynes, The General Theory (1936).
